FROM: Chairman Thomas J. Gleeson o>

DATE: September 9, 2025

RE: September 11, 2026 Open Meeting — Item Nos. 7 & 10

Docket No. 59182; SOAH Docket No. 473-26-10397 — Joint Application of Oncor
Electric Delivery Company LLC and LCRA Transmission Services Corporation to
Amend Their Certificates of Convenience and Necessity for the Big Hill Substation
to Sand Lake Switch 765-kV Transmission Line Project in Crane, Crockett, Irion,
Pecos, Reagan, Reeves, Schleicher, Tom Green, Upton, and Ward Counties;

Docket No. 59475; SOAH Docket No. 473-26-16349 — Joint Application of Oncor
Electric Delivery Company LLC and LCRA Transmission Service Corporation to
Amend Their Certificates of Convenience and Necessity for the Bell County East
Switch to Big Hill Substation 765-kV Transmission Line Project in Bell, Burnet,
Concho, Coryell, Lampasas, Llano, Mason, McCulloch, Menard, Milam, Mills, San
Saba, Schleicher, Tom Green, and Williamson Counties.

A proposal for decision (PFD) was filed on August 20, 2026, by the State Office of
Administrative Hearings (SOAH) in Docket No. 59475, which also addresses a limited set of
consolidated issues from Docket No. 59182. At this time, I believe it is premature to address
whether the recommendations in the PFD should be acted on. Instead, for the reasons outlined
below, I believe we need to remand this proceeding to SOAH for further processing. Because I
believe remand is appropriate, I would not grant oral argument for this week’s open meeting.
Instead, I would defer granting oral argument to a future open meeting date.

Preliminary Order Issues Remain to be Addressed

When a proceeding is referred to SOAH, the Texas Government Code requires the
Commission to “provide to the administrative law judge a list of issues or areas that must be
addressed.”! The law also provides that “the commission may identify and provide to the
administrative law judge at any time additional issues or areas that must be addressed.”?

The Commission referred this proceeding to SOAH on March 30, 2026. In the order of
referral and preliminary order, the Commission included 21 issues and subissues for the

1 Texas Government Code § 2003.049(e).
2 Td.

 administrative law judges (ALIs) to address.? The issues included were the standard issues that
must be addressed in all transmission line CCN proceedings.

In this case, it appears the PFD filed by the ALIJs is incomplete because it does not address
all of issues identified in the March 30, 2026, preliminary order. Specifically, the PFD does not
provide recommendations on preliminary order issues 11 and 13.

Preliminary Order Issue No. 11

11. Are the proposed transmission facilities necessary to meet state or federal
reliability standards?

Notably, the PFD does not address issue 11 of the preliminary order, which asks whether
the proposed transmission facilities are necessary to meet state or federal reliability standards.*
The ALJs find only that “the Applicants present the Project as one that will import power from
across the state of Texas into the Permian Basin and not that the proposed facilities necessary to
meet state or federal reliability standards.”> This finding is not responsive to preliminary order
issue 11. Issue 11 solicits a recommendation on whether the proposed transmission facilities are
in fact necessary to meet state or federal reliability standards, not how the applicants characterize
the project.

The lack of a recommendation on this issue is puzzling in light of the ALJs’
recommendation that the proposed transmission line be evaluated as a reliability project rather than
an economic project under Commission rules.° Under the Commission’s rules, applications for
transmission line projects must demonstrate need as an economic project—unless the project can
qualify as a reliability project or a resiliency project.” A reliability project is classified as “a
transmission line that is necessary to meet state or federal reliability standards.”* Thus, if the ALJs
found that the transmission facilities in this case should be evaluated as a reliability project, this
necessitates findings on what federal and state reliability standards the transmission facilities are
purportedly addressing.

Thus, as required by issue 11 in the March 30, 2026, preliminary order, the Commission
needs findings on whether this project is required by federal and state reliability standards. In
addressing the question of federal reliability standards, the ALJs should address the specific North
American Electric Reliability Corporation (NERC) reliability standards at issue. Although the
ALJs reference “NERC contingencies” at one point in the findings of fact, the relevant NERC
standards are not defined.’ In addressing this issue, I also believe the ALJs should address whether
failure to comply with the relevant NERC standards would result in violation of federal law,
although this may require additional briefing. Ultimately, the Commission should not make a final
decision on need without a recommendation from the ALJs regarding whether the proposed
facilities are necessary to comply with federal (and state) standards.

 Preliminary Order Issue No. 13

13. What is the estimated congestion cost savings for consumers that may result
from the proposed transmission facilities considering both current and future
expected congestion levels and the ability of the proposed transmission facilities
to reduce those congestion levels?

The PFD also does not address preliminary order issue 13 regarding the estimated
congestion cost savings for consumers resulting from the proposed transmission facilities.!° The
PFD mentions issue 13 but finds that the analysis for cost to consumers and congestion cost savings
was not required because it applies to economic projects rather than reliability projects under the
Commission’s rules.!! It also finds that applicants did not submit evidence regarding the estimated
congestion cost savings.!?

Nevertheless, the Commission’s rule and the preliminary order were inclusive on the
grounds for demonstrating need. If the ALJs find that the transmission line fails to establish need
as a reliability project, the question remains of whether need was demonstrated as an economic
project. Thus, the ALJs must address issue 13 regarding whether there are estimated congestion
cost savings for consumers that may result from the proposed transmission facilities.

Under 16 TAC § 22.262(c), the Commission may remand a proceeding to SOAH for
further consideration. In this case, I believe remand is necessary because the ALJs did not provide
recommendations on all the preliminary order issues. On remand, the SOAH ALJs should fully
address issue numbers 11 and 13 from the Commission’s March 30, 2026, preliminary order. I do
not know that it is necessary to reopen the record to address these issues, but I would defer to the
judgment of the SOAH ALJs on this point. Consistent with the rule, a supplemental or amended
PFD may be required to address these additional issues.

Oral Argument Should be Heard at a Later Date

Because I believe remand is appropriate, it would be premature to hear oral argument at
this time. But I still commit to granting oral argument in this case before any final decisions are
made. So, I would defer all the requests for oral argument to be considered for a future open
meeting.

I look forward to discussing this matter with you at the open meeting.
